Colombia’s Engineering & Construction Sector Shows Steady Growth in Q1 2024

Colombia’s Engineering & Construction industry reported modest but steady gains in the first quarter of 2024, continuing its recovery trend from the previous year. According to data released by the Colombian Association of Engineering and Construction (ACIC), sector revenues grew by 6.1% year-on-year, reaching COP 12.3 trillion. The industry’s performance was buoyed by ongoing infrastructure projects and a stable pipeline of commercial and residential developments.

Industry stakeholders attribute the growth to sustained investment in public infrastructure and urban renewal projects, particularly in major cities such as Bogotá, Medellín, and Barranquilla. “We are seeing consistent demand for both large-scale public works and private sector construction,” said Laura Peña, executive director of ACIC. “Transport infrastructure upgrades, as well as housing and mixed-use developments, have played a significant role in supporting industry momentum.”

Among the key contributors to the quarter’s results were continued works on the Bogotá Metro expansion, several highway modernization projects, and the initiation of mid-sized residential complexes in Cali and Cartagena. According to ACIC’s report, public sector contracts accounted for nearly 54% of industry revenues in Q1, while private projects represented 46%, reflecting a balanced demand environment.

“Colombia’s macroeconomic stability and predictable regulatory environment have remained attractive to both domestic and foreign investors,” noted Juan Camilo Torres, research analyst at Cifra Construye, a local market intelligence firm. “While global economic uncertainty persists, the sector has managed to navigate these challenges thanks to strong fundamentals and prudent project management.”

Employment figures for the sector also saw a moderate uptick, with ACIC estimating that over 18,000 new jobs were created during the quarter. The union of Construction Workers of Colombia (UNACOL) welcomed the increase, highlighting continued opportunities for skilled and semi-skilled labor. “Our members are seeing more stable work contracts and improved safety standards on sites,” said UNACOL president José Ricardo Londoño.

Looking ahead, industry leaders remain cautiously optimistic. While no major disruptions are forecast, ACIC has emphasized the importance of maintaining investment momentum to ensure ongoing sector health. “We are closely monitoring input costs, especially for imported materials, but so far there have been no significant shortages or price shocks,” Peña added.

With a robust project pipeline and a supportive policy landscape, Colombia’s Engineering & Construction sector appears set for further stable growth through the remainder of 2024.
